title: Rules of Hooks
summary: The **Rules of Hooks** are two rules every Hook must follow: only call Hooks at the **top level** of a component or another Hook, and only call Hooks from **React functions**. Breaking them corrupts how React tracks state.
nestedConcepts: call hooks at the top level

subtopics.title: Call hooks at the top level
subtopics.explanation: Every Hook must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook, before any early return. This guarantees React encounters the same Hook calls in the same sequence on every render. The condition you were tempted to wrap the Hook in belongs in the JSX you render or inside the Hook's own body, never around the call itself.

subtopics.title: No hooks in conditions/loops/nested functions
subtopics.explanation: Calling a Hook inside an if, a for loop, a callback, or after an early return makes the number or order of Hook calls vary between renders. Even a loop with a 'fixed' count is fragile and flagged by the linter. The fix is structural: pull the Hook out to the top level and move the variability into the Hook body or the rendered output.

subtopics.title: Call only from React functions
subtopics.explanation: Hooks may be called only from function components or from other custom Hooks, never from regular JavaScript functions, event handlers, or class components. The reason is that Hook state must attach to a component's fiber, which only exists while a React function is rendering. Outside that context there is nowhere for the state to live, so the call is meaningless.

subtopics.title: Why order matters
subtopics.explanation: React does not track Hooks by the variable names you give them; it tracks them purely by call order, storing each Hook's state in an ordered list on the fiber and reading it back position by position. If a conditional skips a Hook, every later Hook shifts by one slot and receives the wrong stored state, producing corruption or a 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected' error.

subtopics.title: Rendered fewer/more hooks error
subtopics.explanation: When the number of Hooks changes between renders, React's development-time check detects the mismatch and throws 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected' or 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'. This is React surfacing an order violation early rather than letting silently-wrong state ship. Seeing it almost always means a Hook is behind a condition or early return.

subtopics.title: eslint-plugin-react-hooks
subtopics.explanation: The official ESLint plugin enforces the rules statically with two rules: rules-of-hooks flags misplaced Hook calls, and exhaustive-deps verifies effect dependency arrays. Because conditional Hooks are easy to miss in code review, wiring this plugin into the shared config and CI is the most reliable way to scale enforcement across a team without relying on human vigilance.

subtopics.title: Where conditional logic belongs
subtopics.explanation: The rules forbid conditional Hook calls, not conditional behavior. Put the condition inside the Hook body (for example, an early return at the top of a useEffect callback), or render different JSX based on a flag, or split the conditional part into a child component that mounts conditionally and calls its own Hooks unconditionally. The Hook always runs; only what it does varies.

foundations.overview: Hooks like useState and useEffect must be called in the same order on every render. React does not see the names you give your state — it tracks each Hook by the order in which it was called. The Rules of Hooks exist to guarantee that order stays consistent: always call Hooks at the top level, and only from React functions.
foundations.formalDefinition: The Rules of Hooks state: (1) Only call Hooks at the top level of a function component or a custom Hook — never inside conditions, loops, nested functions, or after an early return. (2) Only call Hooks from React function components or from other custom Hooks — not from regular JavaScript functions or class components.
foundations.whyItMatters: React relies on a stable call order to match each Hook call to its stored state across renders. If the order changes between renders, React associates the wrong state with the wrong Hook, producing bugs that range from lost input to crashes. These rules are the contract that keeps Hooks reliable.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture React holding a numbered list of slots for your component: slot 1, slot 2, slot 3. On every render it walks your Hook calls in order and reads slot 1, slot 2, slot 3. If a condition skips a Hook, the list shifts and React hands slot 2's value to what should have been slot 3 — everything after lines up wrong.
foundations.browserPerspective: There is no browser involvement here. The rules govern React's internal bookkeeping (the linked list of Hooks on the component's fiber), which exists only in React's memory. The DOM only ever sees the output of a correctly-rendered component.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every React component that uses Hooks is bound by these rules. In practice the eslint-plugin-react-hooks lint rule catches violations as you type, so most developers experience the rules as red squiggles in their editor rather than runtime crashes.
foundations.businessImpact: A conditionally-called Hook can ship a subtle bug that only appears for certain users or data, corrupting form input or crashing a screen. Catching it at lint time instead of in production protects conversion and avoids costly incident response.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Following the rules keeps state predictable and makes components easy to reason about. The lint rule also enforces correct effect dependencies, preventing stale-closure and infinite-loop bugs before they reach review.
foundations.performanceImpact: The rules themselves add no runtime cost — they are enforced statically by the linter and a development-time check. By preventing incorrect re-renders and effect loops, following them avoids the performance pathologies that broken Hook ordering can cause.
commonUseCases: Enforcing top-level Hook calls so state is tracked correctly
Letting the linter (eslint-plugin-react-hooks) auto-flag misplaced Hooks
Keeping conditional logic inside the Hook rather than around the Hook call
Verifying effect dependency arrays via the exhaustive-deps rule

commonMisconceptions.myth: It's fine to call a Hook inside an if as long as the condition rarely changes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Any condition that can change between renders shifts the Hook order and corrupts state. Always call the Hook unconditionally and put the condition inside it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: React tracks Hooks by the variable name I assign them to.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React tracks Hooks purely by call order, not by name. That's exactly why the order must be identical on every render.

visualExplorer.title: Why Hook order must stay stable
visualExplorer.caption: Follow how React matches each Hook call to a numbered slot — and how a conditional Hook shifts every slot after it out of alignment.

config.intro: React stores Hook state in an ordered list and matches calls to slots by position. Walk through why a conditional Hook breaks that.

steps.name: React keeps numbered slots
steps.detail: On the first render React records each Hook call in order: useState -> slot 1, useState -> slot 2, useEffect -> slot 3.

steps.name: Order is the only key
steps.detail: React does not use your variable names. It re-reads the slots in the same order on the next render, assuming the same calls happen in the same sequence.

steps.name: A conditional Hook appears
steps.detail: Someone wraps the second useState in an if. On the first render the condition is true, so slot 2 exists.

steps.name: The condition flips
steps.detail: On a later render the condition is false, so the second useState is skipped. Now there is no slot 2 call where React expected one.

steps.name: Slots shift and mismatch
steps.detail: The useEffect that was slot 3 now reads slot 2's stored value. State is matched to the wrong Hook — corrupted state or a crash.

steps.name: The rule prevents it
steps.detail: Calling every Hook at the top level, unconditionally, guarantees the same calls in the same order every render, so the slots always line up.

interactiveExamples.title: The correct pattern: Hooks at the top level
interactiveExamples.explanation: All Hooks are called unconditionally at the top of the component. The conditional logic lives in the JSX, not around the Hook calls, so the order is always identical.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Both useState calls run every render; the button toggles a welcome message via conditional JSX, not a conditional Hook.

interactiveExamples.title: Move the condition inside the Hook
interactiveExamples.explanation: Instead of calling useEffect conditionally, always call it and put the condition inside. The Hook still runs in the same slot every render, but its body only acts when the condition is true.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The interval starts and stops, but useEffect is always called — the condition lives inside it.

codeLab.title: Fix a Hook called after an early return
codeLab.instructions: This component calls useState after an early return, so the Hook is skipped when the user is logged out — breaking the rules. Refactor so every Hook is called at the top level, before any return, and the condition only affects the JSX.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Logging in shows a welcome message, with both Hooks always called at the top level.
hints: Move every useState call above any return statement.
An early return is allowed — but only after all Hooks have been called.
The condition should decide what to render, never which Hooks run.

debuggingLab.title: A Hook called inside a condition breaks state
debuggingLab.symptom: When showName is true everything looks fine, but toggling it off and on scrambles the values — the name shows up where the count should be, or React throws 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: useState for name is called inside an if. On the first render (showName true) React records slots in the order: showName, name, count. When showName flips to false, the name Hook is skipped, so count now lands in the slot React reserved for name. React detects the changed Hook count and warns 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected', and state is matched to the wrong Hook.
commonMistakes: Calling a Hook inside an if, loop, or after an early return.
Assuming React tracks Hooks by name — it tracks them purely by call order.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move the name useState to the top level so all three Hooks are always called in the same order, and use conditional JSX for the visibility.

theory.question: What are the two Rules of Hooks?
theory.directAnswer: First, only call Hooks at the top level — never inside conditions, loops, nested functions, or after an early return. Second, only call Hooks from React function components or from custom Hooks, not from regular JavaScript functions or class components.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two constraints on where and how you may call Hooks so React can track their state correctly.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: React matches each Hook call to its stored state by call order, so the order must be identical on every render; and Hook state only makes sense inside a rendering React function.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Calling Hooks unconditionally at the top level guarantees the same sequence of calls every render. Calling them only from React functions ensures there is a component fiber to attach the state to.

theory.whyImportant: These rules are the foundation of reliable Hook behaviour; violating them causes subtle state-corruption bugs, so interviewers check that you both know the rules and understand why they exist.
theory.realWorldExample: Putting useState inside an if to 'save a Hook when a feature is off' silently corrupts the state of every Hook declared after it.

nestedTopics.title: Top-level only
nestedTopics.explanation: No Hooks inside conditions, loops, nested functions, or after early returns — the call order must never change between renders.

nestedTopics.title: React functions only
nestedTopics.explanation: Hooks may be called from function components and custom Hooks, never from plain functions, event handlers, or class components.

nestedTopics.title: Why order matters
nestedTopics.explanation: React stores Hook state in an ordered list and matches calls to it by position, not by name.

followUps.question: Can I call a Hook inside a loop if the count is fixed?
followUps.answer: It is strongly discouraged and the linter flags it. Even a 'fixed' count is fragile; prefer restructuring so Hooks are called unconditionally at the top level.

followUps.question: Where can I put conditional logic then?
followUps.answer: Inside the Hook's body (e.g. an early return inside useEffect) or in the JSX you render — never around the Hook call itself.

theory.question: Why does React require Hooks to be called in the same order every render?
theory.directAnswer: Because React identifies each Hook by its call order, not by name. It stores Hook state in an ordered list on the component's fiber and reads it back position by position on each render. If the order changes, React associates the wrong state with the wrong Hook, causing corruption or a 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected' error.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An explanation of React's internal Hook-tracking mechanism.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Hooks have no names visible to React — useState('Ada') and useState(0) are indistinguishable to it except by the order in which they run.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On the first render React appends each Hook's state to a linked list. On every subsequent render it walks that list in order, returning each stored value to the corresponding call. A consistent order is what keeps that mapping correct.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding the order-based mechanism is what turns the rules from arbitrary syntax restrictions into something you can reason about and never accidentally break.
theory.realWorldExample: Skipping a useState behind a condition shifts every later Hook by one slot, so a number can suddenly appear where a string was expected.

nestedTopics.title: The Hook linked list
nestedTopics.explanation: React keeps Hook state in an ordered structure on the fiber, traversed in call order each render.

nestedTopics.title: No name tracking
nestedTopics.explanation: Variable names are irrelevant to React; only call position identifies a Hook.

nestedTopics.title: The development-time check
nestedTopics.explanation: React compares the number of Hooks between renders and warns when it changes, surfacing order violations early.

followUps.question: What error appears when the order changes?
followUps.answer: Commonly 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected' or 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render', depending on which direction the count shifted.

followUps.question: Does this also apply to custom Hooks?
followUps.answer: Yes. A custom Hook calls Hooks too, so its calls participate in the same ordered list and must also be unconditional.

scenario.question: A teammate wraps a useState in an if to 'avoid creating state when a feature flag is off'. The app works in their tests but crashes for some users with 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected'. What's wrong and how do you advise them?
scenario.directAnswer: The conditional useState changes the number and order of Hooks between renders. When the flag flips, React finds a different Hook count and throws. The fix is to always call the Hook at the top level and let the feature flag control the rendered output or the Hook's internal behaviour, not whether the Hook runs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A classic Rules-of-Hooks violation hidden behind a feature flag whose value can change.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Their tests only exercised one flag value, so the order never changed during testing; real users toggled the flag, changing the Hook order at runtime.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Hooks are matched to state by call order. A flag-gated Hook adds or removes a call, shifting every later Hook and triggering React's mismatch check.

scenario.whyImportant: Feature-flag-gated Hooks are a real, sneaky source of production crashes; this scenario tests whether you can diagnose order-related Hook bugs.

nestedTopics.title: Stable call order
nestedTopics.explanation: The number and sequence of Hook calls must be identical on every render regardless of flags or data.

nestedTopics.title: Where the condition belongs
nestedTopics.explanation: Gate the rendered JSX or the logic inside the Hook, never the Hook call itself.

followUps.question: How could this have been caught earlier?
followUps.answer: eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags Hooks inside conditionals at lint time; enabling it in CI would have caught the violation before merge.

coding.question: Refactor this component so it follows the Rules of Hooks: it currently calls useEffect only when active is true.
coding.thoughtProcess: The fix is never to wrap the Hook in a condition. I call useEffect unconditionally and move the condition inside the effect body, returning early when inactive. The Hook still occupies the same slot every render, so the order is stable.
coding.lineByLine: useState declarations stay at the top level. useEffect is always called — the active check lives inside its body with an early return, so the Hook runs in the same slot every render while only acting when active. The dependency array [active] re-runs the effect when the flag changes.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per render for Hook bookkeeping.

alternativeApproaches.title: Conditional rendering of a child
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Render a child component only when active is true and put the effect in that child. The effect's mount/unmount then naturally tracks the condition, while each component still calls its Hooks unconditionally.

followUps.question: Why not just wrap useEffect in if (active)?
followUps.answer: That would call the Hook conditionally, changing the Hook order between renders and breaking React's state tracking.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Treat the Rules of Hooks as a non-negotiable invariant. Structure components so all Hooks sit at the top, before any early return, with conditions expressed in JSX or inside Hook bodies. This keeps components predictable and makes them safe to refactor.
productionDeepDive.performance: The rules are enforced statically and at development time, so they cost nothing at runtime. Following them prevents the real performance problems caused by broken ordering — corrupted state forcing remounts, or conditionally-skipped effects leaking timers and listeners.
productionDeepDive.security: No direct security surface, but corrupted Hook state can cause a component to render the wrong user's data into the DOM. Keeping state tracking correct is part of rendering the right data to the right person.
productionDeepDive.scaling: On a large team the linter is what scales the rules. Enable eslint-plugin-react-hooks (rules-of-hooks and exhaustive-deps) in the shared config and run it in CI so every contributor is protected without relying on code-review vigilance.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Components that always call their Hooks at the top level are easy to read and refactor — you can move logic without fear of changing Hook order. Inconsistent ordering, by contrast, creates fragile code that breaks when conditions change.
productionDeepDive.observability: React surfaces violations loudly: in development it warns 'Rendered fewer/more hooks than during the previous render', and the linter underlines misplaced Hooks in the editor. React DevTools shows the Hook list per component, helping confirm the order is stable.

caseStudies.problem: Early Hook adopters hit intermittent 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected' crashes from Hooks placed inside conditionals and early returns.
caseStudies.solution: Enabled eslint-plugin-react-hooks in CI, which flagged every violation and pushed conditions into JSX or Hook bodies.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A wave of lint fixes upfront vs eliminating a whole class of runtime crashes.
caseStudies.lessons: Automated linting is the most reliable enforcement of the Rules of Hooks; humans miss conditional Hooks during review.

steps.title: Find the violations

steps.checkpoint: The lint output names each conditional or post-return Hook.

steps.title: Move Hooks to the top level
steps.instructions: Lift every flagged Hook above all returns and express the condition in JSX or inside the Hook body.
steps.checkpoint: All components pass the rules-of-hooks rule.

steps.instructions: Turn on the exhaustive-deps rule and fix the effect dependency arrays it flags.

keyTakeaways: Rule 1: only call Hooks at the top level — never in conditions, loops, nested functions, or after an early return.
Rule 2: only call Hooks from React function components or custom Hooks.
React tracks Hooks by call order, not by name, so the order must be identical every render.
Put conditions inside the Hook body or in your JSX, never around the Hook call.
Enable eslint-plugin-react-hooks (rules-of-hooks and exhaustive-deps) to catch violations automatically.
